title: Electron pairs that survive the heat: a step towards room-temperature superconductors
dek: A study of a copper-oxide compound suggests one of the two conditions for superconductivity can hold at room temperature.

article: Scientists have found that one of the two conditions needed for superconductivity - electricity flowing with no resistance at all - may be met even at room temperature. The finding, published in the journal Science on 5 November, does not create a room-temperature superconductor, but it narrows down what is standing in the way.

Ordinary wires waste energy: as electrons travel, they bump into the material and lose some of their energy as heat. In a superconductor, that loss disappears. The catch is that known superconductors work only when they are cooled to extreme cold; some need liquid helium at about -260°C.
Superconductivity needs two things. First, electrons must team up into so-called Cooper pairs. Second, the pairs must move in step with one another, a property physicists call phase coherence.

Researchers from Utrecht, Leiden and Munich studied a copper-oxide compound known as Bi-2212, one of a family of materials that superconduct at relatively high temperatures. They built equipment that could tell apart electric current carried by single electrons from current carried by pairs.

Their measurements showed that pairs form well above the temperature at which the material actually becomes a superconductor. The team concluded that the "glue" binding the electrons together is strong enough to hold them at room temperature.

That shifts the search. If pairing is not the bottleneck, the real problem may be getting the pairs to move together. One research leader, Ingmar Swart, called the result good news, because without stable pairs, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.

Important caveats remain. The measurements themselves were made under extreme cooling; the room-temperature claim is an inference about the strength of the binding. And phase coherence, the second condition, is still unexplained at higher temperatures.

The prize would be enormous: superconductors that work without cooling could transform power grids, magnetic-levitation trains and quantum computers. For now, scientists have found one piece of the puzzle and a clearer picture of the piece still missing.

tasks.q: Which headline best sums up the WHOLE article?
options: Electron pairs may survive at room temperature, but superconductors still need cold
Room-temperature superconductors have finally been invented
Power grids will stop wasting energy next year
tasks.explain: B is the classic overclaim - paragraph 1 says the study "does not create" one. C is a single detail (paragraph 4). D is never promised (paragraph 8 says "could").

tasks.q: Follow the article's logic: put these steps in order (paragraphs 2-6).
items: Superconductors only work when they are extremely cold
Superconductivity needs pairs AND pairs moving in step
Scientists measure current from single electrons versus pairs
They find pairs form well above the superconducting temperature
So the main problem may be making the pairs move together
tasks.explain: Problem → the two conditions → the experiment → the result → what it means. Many science news stories follow this shape.

tasks.q: Scan the article: what does each term refer to?
tasks.explain: Writers often define a technical term right after it, using "so-called" or a comma: look for those signals.

statements.text: In a superconductor, no energy is lost as heat from resistance.
statements.explain: Paragraph 2: "In a superconductor, that loss disappears."

statements.text: The team carried out its measurements at room temperature.
statements.explain: Paragraph 7: the measurements were made under extreme cooling.

statements.text: Scientists now fully understand phase coherence at high temperatures.
statements.explain: Paragraph 7: it "is still unexplained at higher temperatures".

statements.text: The researchers will test other copper oxides next year.

tasks.q: According to the article, what is now most likely the main obstacle to room-temperature superconductors?
options: Getting electron pairs to move in step
Getting electrons to form pairs at all
tasks.explain: Paragraph 6: "If pairing is not the bottleneck, the real problem may be getting the pairs to move together." B is the opposite of the finding.

options: the strongest part of a system
tasks.explain: Like the narrow neck of a bottle, it is the point that slows everything down. The sentence contrasts it with "the real problem".

tasks.q: What is the main purpose of paragraph 7?
options: To stop readers from overstating the result
To explain how superconductors save energy
To argue that the study was badly done
tasks.explain: "Important caveats remain" signals limits. D goes too far - pointing out limits is not saying the work was bad.

write.prompt: Why do scientists care so much about superconductors that work without cooling? Write 2-3 sentences in English, giving one example from the article and one of your own.
write.sample: Superconductors without cooling could transform power grids, because no energy would be lost as heat. I think they could also make MRI machines cheaper, since today these machines need very cold liquid helium.
